clue.text: Brass perhaps gives power masons fancy

indicators.note: fancy as a verb hints at letters reimagined, so the clue's power and masons are rearranged

parts.note: P is the standard abbreviation for power in physics
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that brass, as a power symbol, is something stonemasons like.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fancy' shuffles P (power) with MASONS. Sampson Brass is the crooked lawyer in Dickens's The Old Curiosity Shop, so 'Brass perhaps' points to someone with that first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Sampson Brass is a Dickens character, so Brass is one example of a man with this first name.

clue.text: "What woeful stuff this madrigal would be, / In some starved hackney -, or me?" (Pope)

definitions.text: "What woeful stuff this madrigal would be, / In some starved hackney -, or me?" (Pope)

parts.words: "What woeful stuff this madrigal would be, / In some starved hackney -, or me?" (Pope)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: the missing word in Pope's couplet is a poet who writes fourteen-line verses, mocked as a hack

explanation.surface: A couplet from Alexander Pope with a word missing, sneering at a hired poet.
explanation.walkthrough: The lines come from Pope's poem in the voice of a lady of quality; the solver supplies the missing word from knowledge of the couplet and the letter count.
explanation.definitionFit: The blank in Pope's couplet names a poet who turns out fourteen-line poems, here a hack writer for hire.

clue.text: What Winchester wrote about everything that's poor in Government

parts.note: poor as in shabby or stingy means mean
taken as written

explanation.surface: A remark on Winchester's book about everything that goes wrong in government.
explanation.walkthrough: Simon Winchester wrote The Meaning of Everything, a history of the Oxford English Dictionary; 'that's' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Simon Winchester's OED history is titled The Meaning of Everything, so its subject is the sense of words.

clue.text: Movement that delays April's appearance?

parts.note: read as a calendar joke: if the third month dragged its feet, the fourth would come late; really a solemn processional pace

explanation.surface: A whimsical question about what could hold back the arrival of spring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Movement' suggests a musical movement or politics; the second word is the month before April, and the whole is a stately military pace.
explanation.definitionFit: A funeral or ceremonial pace is a measured parade step; read literally, a sluggish third month would postpone April.

clue.text: Definitely not an Italian composer? Definitely so!

definitions.meaning: a forbidden thing, something that must never be done
Luigi ... was an Italian avant-garde composer

explanation.walkthrough: The closing 'Definitely so!' is a joke: the solver asks whether the answer is an Italian composer, and it is. Luigi Nono (1924-90) was a leading post-war Italian composer.
explanation.definitionFit: A forbidden act is colloquially an emphatic prohibition, and Luigi Nono bore the same surname.

clue.text: French composer substituting a bit of Handel for last two notes in his oratorio

indicators.note: substituting tells us one piece of the composer's name is swapped out for another letter

parts.note: Olivier Messiaen was a French composer

indicators.note: a bit of Handel is just a small part of the name, its first letter

explanation.surface: A French composer's name is tweaked with a touch of Handel to name a famous oratorio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for last two notes' names the letters replaced: the final EN of MESSIAEN gives way to H, the first letter of Handel. 'his' in the definition refers back to Handel.
explanation.definitionFit: Handel's best-known oratorio, first performed in Dublin in 1742, is titled after the Christian saviour.

clue.text: Logic you must both endlessly broadcast in studying 4, 6, 11 13, 14 etc

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters are strewn into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: both endlessly says each of the two words you and must loses its final letter

explanation.surface: An instruction to spread logic far and wide when studying a list of crossword entries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'both endlessly' trims YOU to YO and MUST to MUS; 'broadcast' then shuffles LOGIC + YO + MUS. The cross-references are all musical: a composer, a scena, Enigma Variations, Elgar.
explanation.definitionFit: The academic study of music covers composers, operatic scenes and works such as Elgar's variations, the entries cited.

clue.text: Occasionally sacred number with aria finally

definitions.text: Occasionally sacred number with aria finally

indicators.note: occasionally means now and then, so only every other letter of sacred is taken
finally points to the last letter of aria

explanation.surface: A remark that a sacred musical number sometimes comes with an aria at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Occasionally' takes S, C, E from sacred; add N and the A that ends aria. The whole clue also describes the answer: an operatic number built round an aria.
explanation.definitionFit: In opera this is a dramatic solo number, often recitative leading to an aria, so the whole clue describes it.

clue.text: Fancy one getting one of the possible 13 on 11

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: 13 across is a word for versions, so one version on the entry at 11 is a rearrangement of its letters

parts.note: the entry at 11 across, the name of Elgar's theme

explanation.surface: Picture one person imagining a solution to Elgar's famous musical riddle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one of the possible 13 on 11' reads as 'one of the possible Variations on Enigma': a rearrangement of ENIGMA. Put I in front.
explanation.definitionFit: To fancy something is to suppose or picture it, a synonym of conceiving in the mind.

clue.text: Repeatedly visit Leigh about start of Autumn

indicators.note: about means going round, so the poet's surname encloses the next piece

parts.note: Leigh Hunt was a Romantic poet and essayist, friend of Keats

indicators.note: start of Autumn means its first letter

explanation.surface: A suggestion to call often on someone named Leigh at the beginning of autumn.
explanation.walkthrough: Leigh Hunt (1784-1859) was an English poet and critic; his surname goes around A, the first letter of Autumn.
explanation.definitionFit: To frequent a place, calling often, is a synonym; ghosts are said to do it too.

clue.text: A marshytree?

parts.note: read as a tree from a bog, but split as a Marsh-y tree: a New Zealand tree whose name the crime writer Marsh bore as her first name

explanation.surface: A question about a tree that grows in wet ground.
explanation.walkthrough: Ngaio Marsh was a New Zealand detective novelist; her first name is also that of a small native New Zealand tree, so the tree is 'Marsh-y'.
explanation.definitionFit: The New Zealand tree shares its name with novelist Ngaio Marsh, making it the tree with a Marsh connection.

clue.text: Transylvanian savagely set on Frau

indicators.note: savagely suggests the words are mauled and torn apart into a new order

explanation.surface: A Transylvanian creature viciously attacks a German woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'savagely' shuffles SET ON FRAU. Nosferatu is the vampire of Murnau's 1922 film, based on Dracula, who comes from Transylvania.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1922 film vampire Count Orlok is a Dracula figure, so he is a creature from that Romanian region.

clue.text: One man with energy, Turing, finally cracked it

definitions.text: One man with energy, Turing, finally cracked it

indicators.note: cracked means broken apart, so the pieces gathered are rearranged

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
taken as written
E is the symbol for energy in physics

indicators.note: finally takes the last letter of Turing

explanation.surface: Alan Turing, one energetic man, broke the German cipher machine.
explanation.walkthrough: I + MAN + E + G (last of Turing) are shuffled by 'cracked'. The whole clue is also a description: Turing's team at Bletchley Park broke the German cipher.
explanation.definitionFit: The German wartime cipher machine was broken at Bletchley Park by Turing's team, so the whole clue describes it.

clue.text: Chap with a razor mostly arrived at the top of the queue after officer

indicators.note: after says the next pieces follow the abbreviation for the officer

parts.note: OC is Officer Commanding

indicators.note: mostly means all but the last letter of the word for arrived

parts.note: arrived means came

parts.words: at the top of the queue
parts.note: at the top of the queue means first, written 1st, with the 1 read as the letter I

explanation.surface: A man with a razor almost reached the front of the line behind an officer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at the top of the queue' is first, written 1ST, and the digit 1 stands in as I. The razor is the philosopher William of Ockham's principle of economy, not a barber's blade.
explanation.definitionFit: A follower of William of Ockham applies his principle of economy, known as his razor.

clue.text: What one air on stave mostly can be turned into?

definitions.text: What one air on stave mostly can be turned into?

indicators.note: can be turned into says the gathered letters are converted into a new arrangement

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
taken as written

indicators.note: mostly drops the last letter of stave

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A question: what may a single tune written on a stave be developed into?
explanation.walkthrough: I + AIR ON + STAV are shuffled by 'can be turned into'. The whole also describes the answer: one tune on a stave can be worked into many versions.
explanation.definitionFit: A theme is developed into modified versions of itself in a musical form, so one air becomes many.

clue.text: Lear confused about heart of Kingdom and who fashioned it

indicators.note: about means around, so the jumbled king surrounds the next letter
confused means muddled, so the letters of Lear are rearranged
heart of picks the middle letter of Kingdom

explanation.surface: King Lear in a muddle about the centre of his kingdom, and who created him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confused' turns LEAR into ELAR, which goes 'about' G, the middle letter of Kingdom. 'it' is 11 across, the theme Elgar composed.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Elgar composed the Enigma Variations, so he is the maker of the theme at 11 across.

clue.text: After start of afternoon mostly every dance is over in quick time

indicators.note: After says the remaining pieces follow the opening letter
start of afternoon is its first letter
is over means turned over, so the words for every and dance read backwards
mostly drops the final letter of the synonym

parts.note: every means ever-y, so ever is every less its end
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: Every dance after the start of the afternoon is finished at a brisk pace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is over' turns both the shortened 'every' and the dance round, and 'After' puts them behind the opening A. Alla breve is a musical marking for two minim beats to a bar.
explanation.definitionFit: The musical marking calls for two minim beats per bar, a brisk tempo.

clue.text: Celebrity returning about to set up a party in a Scottish village

indicators.note: about means around, so the reversed bigwig wraps the following pieces
returning means coming back, so the word for celebrity reads backwards

parts.note: a nob is a notable or toff, a big name
to rig is to set up or fix
a do is a party, so a do gives ADO

explanation.surface: A returning star is about to organise a party in a Highland village.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' turns the toff round, and 'about' wraps that reversal around the fixing word and the party. Brigadoon is the Scottish village in the Lerner and Loewe musical that appears once a century.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lerner and Loewe musical is set in a magical Highland hamlet of that name.

clue.text: In zeal mostly mixes terms indiscriminately

indicators.note: indiscriminately means at random, so the letters are thrown together in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: mostly drops the last letter of terms

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone in a fervour jumbles their words without care.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' cuts TERMS to TERM; 'indiscriminately' shuffles MIXES + TERM. 'In' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Fanatical fervour carried beyond moderation is the excess the answer names; zeal is a near synonym.

clue.text: Reflecting about a nymph in capital of Greece

parts.note: re means about, as in a letter heading
Echo was the nymph in Greek myth who could only repeat others' words
taken as written

indicators.note: capital of Greece means its first letter

explanation.surface: Thinking about a mythological nymph while in Athens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital of Greece' looks like Athens but is just the letter G. Echo, the nymph who pined for Narcissus, is a fair clue for the sound that bounces back.
explanation.definitionFit: Sound that reflects off a surface repeats back, which is a synonym for resounding again.

clue.text: At start of enquiry a word for revenge Lestrade thought was a woman; what a pain!

indicators.note: start of enquiry is its first letter

parts.words: word for revenge Lestrade thought was a woman
parts.note: in A Study in Scarlet, RACHE is written in blood; Lestrade thinks it is an unfinished Rachel, but it is German for revenge

explanation.surface: Investigating a case where the detective mistook a word, causing a real headache.
explanation.walkthrough: In Conan Doyle's A Study in Scarlet, Inspector Lestrade reads RACHE on a wall as the start of 'Rachel'; Holmes says it is German for revenge. 'At' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An ache inside the ear is literally a pain, and figuratively an annoyance.

clue.text: Small figure giving directions in Stephen King's thriller

indicators.note: in places the directions inside the novel's title

parts.note: It is Stephen King's 1986 horror novel about a killer clown
N, S and E are compass directions

explanation.surface: Stephen King's novel includes a small map giving directions.
explanation.walkthrough: IT, Stephen King's novel, takes three compass points inside it. 'giving' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A small picture set within a larger page or map is called by that name.

clue.text: Pay out about a note in Harding's wages

indicators.note: about means around, so the word for paying out goes round the note

parts.note: to pay out money is to spend
ti is a note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: Someone pays out money on a banknote from Harding's earnings.
explanation.walkthrough: Septimus Harding is the clergyman of Trollope's The Warden, so his income is a clerical salary. 'note' looks like money but is the sol-fa note.
explanation.definitionFit: A clergyman's fixed salary is called by that name, and Harding in Trollope is a clergyman.

clue.text: One who could have played in Carnival of the Animals, with zoo represented about start of recital

definitions.text: One who could have played in Carnival of the Animals

explanation.surface: A pianist who could have performed Saint-Saëns's zoological suite, with a zoo pictured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'represented' shuffles WITH ZOO, which goes 'about' R from recital. Saint-Saëns's suite includes a movement called Pianists, so a virtuoso pianist could be one of its 'animals'.
explanation.definitionFit: Vladimir Horowitz was a virtuoso pianist, and Saint-Saëns includes pianists among the creatures of his suite.

clue.text: End of mystery in hard novel-a problem for Hercules

explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' turns HARD into HDRA; 'in' puts Y, the last letter of mystery, inside. 'novel' looks like a book but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The many-headed serpent of Lerna was the second of Hercules's twelve labours.

clue.text: Wanderer changing direction to reach global festival

explanation.definitionFit: WOMAD, World of Music, Arts and Dance, is an international music festival founded by Peter Gabriel.

clue.text: Ladette, one of the possible 13 on 11

clue.text: A famous Whig, reportedly, a person of little intelligence

explanation.walkthrough: Edmund Burke (1729-97) was an Anglo-Irish Whig statesman. 'Berk' is British slang for an idiot.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a fool or idiot, an insult to someone dim-witted.

clue.text: Break down and stop scoring?

definitions.meaning: to undo or cease writing music, scoring being writing for orchestra

explanation.walkthrough: 'scoring' looks like a sporting term but means writing musical scores; the prefix de- reverses composing.
explanation.definitionFit: To rot is to break down, and jokingly to un-write music is to stop scoring.

clue.text: After honour's returned I start to look daggers

clue.text: 007 mostly unhappy about things that need to be done

clue.text: "Or else my — stands on brittle glass" (Richard IIl)

parts.words: "Or else my — stands on brittle glass" (Richard IIl)
